I pick **Candidate 4**. These are rough mental estimates, not an exact simulation, and Candidate 4 leads the next-best plan by only about 100. That edge is real in the averages but small compared with the day-to-day randomness.

**What the candidates are.** Each plan is the demand forecast for the arrival day multiplied by a fixed factor:
- Candidates 0 and 1 use 1.2. Candidate 0 trims the tail.
- Candidate 7 uses 1.2 for item 0 and 1.0 for item 1.
- Candidate 3 uses 1.1 and Candidate 2 uses 1.0, both ordering daily.
- Candidate 4 (×1.0) and Candidate 6 (×1.1) order every 2 days. Candidate 5 (×1.1) orders every 3 days.

**Shortfalls at the start are the same for everyone.** The starting stock runs out before the first order arrives on day 3 (item 0) or day 4 (item 1). So every plan builds its buffer from zero.

**Why 1.0 beats 1.1 and 1.2.** Because orders don't react to stock, leftovers pile up like a random walk. Average demand is about 1.046 × forecast.
- **×1.2:** about 15% of the forecast is surplus every day. Stock grows to the shelf-life limit and to the 212-unit capacity. Expiry, end-of-month waste (about 2,300) and holding (about 1,900) add up to more than 4,000 lost. Candidates 0, 1 and partly 7 are out.
- **×1.1:** shortfalls cost about 310. But about 44 units of item 0 and 53 of item 1 are left unsold at the end (about 1,120 wasted), plus about 1,000 in holding. Total loss is about 2,400.
- **×1.0:** shortfalls cost about 1,000 (about 41 units of item 0 at 14 each, about 49 of item 1 at 9 each). End waste is about 350 and holding about 380. Total loss is about 1,750, the best of the three.

**Ordering every 2 days vs daily (Candidate 4 vs Candidate 2).**
- **Fees:** 14 order days instead of 27 saves 546.
- **Extra holding:** next day's demand sits overnight. For item 0 that is 295 unit-nights, about 207. For item 1 it is 341 unit-nights, about 239. Together about 445.
- **Shortfall risk:** about the same, since the low point is still just before each delivery.
- **Net:** about +100 for Candidate 4.

**Ordering every 3 days (Candidate 5).** It saves 756 in fees, but extra holding is about 980, and the large deliveries come close to the capacity limit. It loses.

**Candidate 6 vs Candidate 4.** Same schedule, but ×1.1 is about 680 worse than ×1.0.

I picked **candidate 4**. It orders roughly the forecast amount every two days, and it beats the daily plan at the same quantities (candidate 2) by about 200–300. These are rough mental estimates.

**What every plan loses the same way.** The starting stock of 33 units of product 0 is gone by day 1. The 46 units of product 1 are gone by day 3. No delivery can arrive before day 3 or 4, so all candidates pay the same early-shortage penalties.

**How much to order.** Every plan is fixed in advance and never reacts to actual demand. Each unit ordered is either sold at some point or wasted, because of the shelf life or because it is left over at the end. In profit terms:
- Product 0: each extra unit costs 11. Each shortage avoided is worth 25 (18 in lost sale plus the 7 penalty).
- Product 1: each extra unit costs 12. Each shortage avoided is worth 21.

Roughly, ordering 10% above forecast instead of exactly the forecast plays out like this:

| Product | Extra units bought | Extra cost | Shortages avoided | Value recovered | Extra storage cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | ~58 | ~640 | ~25 | ~625 | ~280 |
| 1 | ~70 | ~840 | ~28 | ~590 | ~300 |

So +10% is worse on both products, and +20% is worse still. That rules out candidates 0, 1, 3 and 7 among the daily plans (all ordering 10–20% above forecast on at least one product). It also rules out candidates 6 and 5 among the batch plans.

**How often to order.** Candidate 4 orders the same quantities as candidate 2, but only every second day:
- It places 14 orders instead of 27, which saves about 546 in fixed fees.
- Holding half a cycle of extra stock costs about 450 in storage.
- Shortages happen slightly less often, worth roughly 100.
- The net is in candidate 4's favour, and its peak stock is well under the 212-unit limit.

**Why not every three days.** Candidate 5 saves 756 in fees, but extra storage costs about 935. It also orders 10% too much, so it comes out worse.

**Risk.** Candidates 2 and 4 face about the same uncertainty. Ordering every second day evens out daily demand swings a little, so candidate 4 is no riskier.

**Выбор: кандидат 4.** Я считал в уме по средним значениям, а случайность учитывал грубо, через модель случайного блуждания. Поэтому цифры ниже приблизительные, но соотношения между кандидатами устойчивы.

**1. Из чего состоят планы.** Каждый план пересчитывает прогноз спроса со сдвигом на срок поставки (3 дня у товара 0, 4 дня у товара 1) с каким-то множителем:
- Кандидат 2: ровно прогноз (1,0×), заказ каждый день.
- Кандидат 3: 1,1×, каждый день.
- Кандидаты 0 и 1: 1,2×, каждый день. Кандидат 0 последние четыре заказа делает примерно на 0,9×, кандидат 1 держит 1,2× до конца.
- Кандидат 7: товар 0 на 1,2×, товар 1 на 1,0×, каждый день.
- Кандидат 4: 1,0×, раз в 2 дня (каждый заказ покрывает два дня).
- Кандидат 6: 1,1×, раз в 2 дня.
- Кандидат 5: раз в 3 дня.

**2. Начало у всех одинаковое.** До первых поставок (товар 0 приходит в день 3, товар 1 в день 4) неизбежна нехватка: около 43 единиц товара 0 и около 78 единиц товара 1. От плана это не зависит.

**3. Почему завышенный запас вредит.** Планы не подстраиваются под факт, поэтому расхождение заказов со средним спросом накапливается на складе изо дня в день. Средний спрос составляет около 1,046× прогноза.
- **При 1,0×** склад немного не дотягивает до спроса, примерно на 1 ед./день по каждому товару. Нехватка: около 40–45 ед. товара 0 и около 45 ед. товара 1. Хранение обходится примерно в 270–310 на товар.
- **При 1,1×** нехватка падает примерно на 27–30 ед. на товар, зато закупка растёт. По товару 0 это около 58 ед. (≈640), по товару 1 около 70 ед. (≈835). Хранение примерно удваивается, а излишек в конце пропадает. В сумме это хуже 1,0× примерно на 230 по товару 0 и на 500 по товару 1.
- **При 1,2×** к концу накапливается около 90 ед. товара 0. Чистый проигрыш относительно 1,0× больше 1000 только по одному товару. Поэтому кандидаты 0, 1 и 7 отпадают. Сокращение заказов в конце у кандидата 0 этого не исправляет.

**4. Заказ раз в 2 дня против ежедневного (кандидат 4 против кандидата 2).**
- Экономия на сборе за заказ: 13 × 42 = 546.
- Дополнительное хранение второго дня партии: примерно (268 + 341) × 0,7 ≈ 426.
- Склад не переполняется: в пике около 65 ед. товара плюс остаток, при вместимости 212.
- Денег хватает.
- Итог: кандидат 4 выигрывает примерно 100–150. Кроме того, у него немного меньше нехватка, потому что колебания спроса гасятся за два дня сразу.

**5. Заказ раз в 3 дня (кандидат 5)** хуже. Хранение растёт примерно на 945, а сбор экономит только 756. К тому же партии около 180 ед. рискуют упереться во вместимость склада.

**6. Порядок по ожидаемой прибыли:** 4 > 2 > 6 > 3 > 5, затем 7, 0 и 1 далеко позади.

**Choice: candidate 4.** It orders about the forecast every other day, which saves on order fees and doesn't over-order. All figures below are mental estimates from forecast values plus rough spread estimates, not a simulation.

**Losses every plan shares.** Until the first deliveries arrive, product 0 has 33 units against about 76 demand (days 0–2). Product 1 has 46 against about 124 (days 0–3). Every plan pays these same shortage penalties, so they don't separate the candidates.

**What each plan looks like:**
- **Candidate 2:** orders the forecast exactly, every day.
- **Candidate 3:** about 1.1 × forecast, every day.
- **Candidates 0 and 1:** about 1.2 × forecast, every day. They differ only at the end.
- **Candidate 7:** 1.2 × forecast for product 0, 1.0 × for product 1, every day.
- **Candidate 4:** every other day, each order covering two days at 1.0 × forecast.
- **Candidate 6:** the same every-other-day pattern at about 1.1 × forecast.
- **Candidate 5:** every third day, at about 1.1 × forecast.

**How much to order.**
- **Product 0:** at 1.0 × forecast, supply runs about 4.6% below average demand. Over the horizon that's roughly 40–45 units short, costing about 14 each (lost margin plus penalty).
- **At 1.1 × forecast:** shortages drop to about 18 units. But about 60 extra units are bought, roughly 50 of them are left unsold at the end, and holding costs rise by about 340. My estimate is that 1.0 beats 1.1 by about 350 for product 0.
- **At 1.2 × forecast:** this is clearly worse.
- **Product 1:** margin is only 3, so over-ordering hurts even more. A factor near 1.0 is best here too.

**How often to order.**
- **Every other day vs daily:** it saves 13 orders × 42 = 546. Holding half of each two-day batch for one extra night costs about 13 × 51 units × 0.7 ≈ 464. Stock also arrives ahead of demand, which slightly reduces shortages. Net, it comes out a little ahead of daily ordering.
- **Every third day:** it saves about 756 in order fees, but extra holding is about 930. That makes candidate 5 a net loss.

**Checks on candidate 4.** Cash stays positive: after day 4's order it bottoms out at about 690, so no order gets cut. The warehouse never comes close to its 212-unit limit. The last deliveries arrive on days 28–29, so nothing is paid for and lost after the end.

**Robustness.** Ordering at 1.0 × forecast hedges well against random demand. Some extra stock carries over to later days, and bigger orders mostly end up as leftovers worth nothing at the end.

Ranking: 4 > 2 ≈ 6 > 3 > 5, 7 > 0, 1.

**Choice: candidate 4.** It orders the forecast quantities (1.0×) every two days. That gives the best expected result: the fewest paid order days with no over-ordering. I worked these numbers by hand, so they are rough.

**What each plan is.** Every plan's order covers the forecast for the day it arrives (3 days later for good 0, 4 for good 1), scaled by a factor:
- Candidate 2: 1.0×, ordering every day.
- Candidate 3: 1.1×, every day.
- Candidates 0 and 1: 1.2×, every day. Candidate 1 orders more over the last few days.
- Candidate 7: 1.2× for good 0 and 1.0× for good 1, every day.
- Candidate 4: 1.0×, every two days.
- Candidate 6: 1.1×, every two days.
- Candidate 5: 1.1×, every three days.

**Losses that are the same for every plan.** Starting stock runs short in the first days: good 0 has 33 units against about 80 of demand on days 0–2, and good 1 has 46 against about 124 on days 0–3. Every plan pays this shortfall equally.

**Over-ordering builds up rather than spoiling.** Units are sold oldest first and last 5 days. Ordering a fixed amount every day means a unit only spoils once stock exceeds about four days of deliveries, which almost never happens. So any surplus just piles up: you pay to buy it, pay storage on it every evening, and most of it is still unsold at the end.
- **Good 0** (cost 11, missed sale costs 25: 18 lost revenue plus 7 penalty). I estimated the main costs (buying, missed sales, storage) at about 7,600 for 1.0×, 7,900 for 1.1× and 8,700 for 1.2×. Average demand runs 4.6% above forecast, but at 1.0× the leftovers from slow days cover most of the busy ones.
- **Good 1** (cost 12, missed sale costs 21: 15 lost revenue plus 6 penalty). The same costs come to about 9,500 for 1.0×, 10,000 for 1.1× and 11,100 for 1.2×. This rules out candidates 0, 1, 3, 5 and 6.

**How often to order.**
- Ordering daily means about 27 order days at 42 each, roughly 1,134.
- Ordering every two days means 14 order days, about 588, saving about 546. The extra storage (about half the units sit one more night) costs about 450, so the net gain is about 100.
- Ordering every two days is also more robust to random demand. Each delivery covers two days, so a single busy day rarely empties the shelf, and missed sales drop.
- Ordering every three days (candidate 5) costs about 940 in extra storage against 756 saved, and it also orders 1.1×.
- Storage space never becomes a limit: candidate 4's peak stock is about 130 of 212.

Candidate 2 is second, roughly 100–200 behind. Candidates 7, 3 and 6 follow, and 0, 1 and 5 are last.
